question: A 3-month-old boy presents with generalised hypotonia ('floppy infant'). On examination, he is alert with good eye contact and normal facial expression, but has markedly reduced muscle tone and tongue fasciculations. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in all four limbs. Where is the lesion MOST LIKELY located?

answers.text: Cerebral cortex — central hypotonia from brain injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Central hypotonia (from brain/upper motor neurone) typically presents with preserved or exaggerated deep tendon reflexes (or normal, especially in the acute phase). Crucially, central hypotonia is accompanied by other cortical features — altered consciousness, poor alertness, seizures. This infant is alert with normal cognition, making central hypotonia less likely.

answers.text: Anterior horn cells — peripheral hypotonia (e.g. spinal muscular atrophy)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the classic clinical picture of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) Type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann): a hypotonic but ALERT infant (cognition is normal because the cortex is intact), absent deep tendon reflexes, and tongue fasciculations (lower motor neurone sign). Absent DTRs with hypotonia = peripheral (lower motor neurone) lesion. SMA is caused by anterior horn cell degeneration and is the most important diagnosis to consider.

Thalamic lesions are not a common or classic cause of neonatal/infant hypotonia. The thalamus is not the final common motor pathway — motor output comes from the motor cortex via the corticospinal tract, which synapses on anterior horn cells. Thalamic lesions cause other neurological signs, not isolated hypotonia with absent DTRs.

answers.text: Peripheral nerve — axonal neuropathy causing hypotonia and absent reflexes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Peripheral nerve (neuropathy) can cause hypotonia with absent DTRs, but tongue fasciculations are a LOWER MOTOR NEURONE sign at the anterior horn cell / cranial nerve nucleus level. A pure peripheral neuropathy would not cause tongue fasciculations. The combination of absent DTRs + tongue fasciculations + normal cognition points to anterior horn cell disease (SMA), not isolated peripheral neuropathy.

overallFeedback.feedback: The central vs peripheral distinction in the floppy infant is made by deep tendon reflexes: central hypotonia = normal/exaggerated DTRs + cortical signs (poor alertness, seizures); peripheral hypotonia = absent/reduced DTRs + intact cognition. Tongue fasciculations confirm a lower motor neurone/anterior horn cell lesion. This infant has SMA.

Correct. The diagnostic key in the floppy infant is the status of deep tendon reflexes: ABSENT or reduced DTRs = peripheral (lower motor neurone) lesion; PRESENT or exaggerated DTRs (in the context of hypotonia) = central (upper motor neurone / brain) lesion. An alert infant with absent DTRs and tongue fasciculations = anterior horn cell disease = SMA until proven otherwise.
